Blends

Multi-Peptide Research Blends — United States

A co-lyophilized blend is several compounds freeze-dried together in one vial. GLOW combines GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500; KLOW adds KPV. The remaining blends here pair repair-model compounds in other ratios.

Blends break the usual verification shortcut, and it is worth being precise about why. A purity result on a multi-compound vial describes the material as a whole. It cannot tell you the ratio between the components, which means a blend can return an excellent purity figure while being weighted quite differently from what the label describes. Nothing about the purity number is wrong; it simply does not answer the question a blend raises.

The figure that does is per-component mass — each compound in the vial measured separately against what the label claims for it. That is what is published for every blend batch here: not one blended purity figure, but the measured content of each component, tied to the lot code on the vial. Reconstitution does not separate a blend, so the ratio is fixed at manufacture and cannot be corrected afterwards.

Each component's own product page carries the underlying literature and is linked from every blend. Supplied strictly as laboratory research materials, shipped domestically within the United States.

What to check before buying blends compounds

Purity is half the number. A purity figure tells you what fraction of the powder in the vial is the compound on the label — it tells you nothing about how much powder is in the vial. A lot can assay at 99.8% purity and still be short against its labelled content.

Both numbers are published for every batch here: purity from HPLC, and measured mass against expected content. Match the batch code printed on the vial to the certificate before you rely on either.

Blends research peptides — common questions

Why does a blend certificate look different?
Because purity is defined for a single compound and a blend is a mixture. A blend report identifies and quantifies each component rather than issuing one area-percent figure for the vial. A blend advertised with a single purity number is reporting something that measurement does not produce.
What is actually in GLOW and KLOW?
GLOW combines GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500. KLOW is the same three plus KPV. Component amounts are printed on the product page and on the lot certificate, so what is in the vial can be checked rather than inferred from the name.
When does a blend make more sense than single vials?
When the research follows the combination as published. A blend is one vial and one fill, so it costs less than the components bought separately, but the ratio is fixed at manufacture. Work that varies one component against the others needs single vials.
How is a blend lot verified?
Each component is identified and quantified independently, and measured content is reported per component against that component’s labelled amount. The lot code on the vial matches the code on that report.
